827.title: Sergius of Radonezh
827.hook: a Russian hermit in the forest who shared bread with a bear and founded a great monastery
827.howItsDone: The Russian Orthodox Church honors Sergius of Radonezh as a saint, and the Trinity monastery that grew up around his forest cell bears his name; his story with the bear is told in his Life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monks of Athos, praying in stillness for the light on the mountain, and your line was the light of tabor.

One piece of bread, on a tree stump at the edge of a clearing. Deep in a Russian forest, a young man has built a small wooden cell and a chapel with his own hands. No village nearby, no road worth the name. One day, the old account says, a bear comes out of the trees, hungry, and stands looking at him. He doesn't run. He brings out a piece of his bread and sets it on the stump. The bear eats it and goes away. Then it comes back, again and again. Today: Sergius of Radonezh.
screen: `ONE PIECE OF BREAD ON A STUMP.`
`A BEAR COMES OUT OF THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Sergius is a monk the Russian Orthodox Church honors as a saint, and his story comes down through a Life written by a monk named Epiphanius. As a young man, the Life says, Sergius went into the forest to live alone with God. He chopped his own wood, grew what he could, and prayed. And the bear kept coming. Here's the detail the Life lingers on. Some days Sergius had only one piece of bread, and on those days, the story goes, he gave it to the bear and went hungry himself, rather than send the animal away with nothing. An odd kind of holiness: not a sermon, but a crust, and an empty stomach. Other Christian stories, too, put holy people at peace with wild animals, and Mark's Gospel has a small line about Jesus in the desert, in the King James Bible: "and was with the wild beasts". In these stories the wilderness isn't only danger; it's also where creatures and a person at prayer learn to live side by side. Sergius didn't stay alone. Other monks heard of him and came to live near him, cells went up around his, and a community grew, dedicated to the Holy Trinity. The Life remembers him as a leader who still carried water, baked bread and wore patched clothes. A monastery grew where his cell had been. But the scene that stays is smaller: the stump, the bread, and the bear.

Think of an animal near your life, a pet on the couch, the birds outside, a neighbor's dog, and one small thing it could use: fresh water, a few seeds, a walk, or simply your patience. Sit with that creature in mind, the way Sergius sat at the edge of his clearing. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, let it be in your thoughts, just as it is.
Sergius. A forest hermit of Radonezh honored by the Orthodox Church, who shared his bread with a bear and around whom a community of the Holy Trinity grew.
Your line: bread with the bear. Even when it was the last piece. Day eight hundred twenty-seven, in the books.

828.title: Rublev's Trinity
828.hook: three angels at Abraham's table, with an open place at the table
828.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray before icons such as Rublev's Trinity at home and in church, and copies of it hang in some churches, Orthodox and others, as a picture of the Trinity and of welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sergius fed his last bread to a bear, and your line was bread with the bear.

Three figures sit around a low table. They have wings and long thin staffs, and their heads lean gently toward one another, as if in a quiet conversation. In the center of the table is a single cup. Behind them, a house, a tree, a rock. The colors are soft: gold, deep blue, pale green. Nobody is eating or in a hurry. And at the front of the table, the side nearest you, there's a gap. Room for one more. Tradition says this icon was painted by a monk named Andrei Rublev, for the monastery that grew up around Sergius.

The scene comes from Genesis. Abraham sits at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and in the King James Bible: "he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him". Abraham runs to meet them and bows. He fetches water for their feet, has bread baked and a calf prepared, and stands by them under a tree while they eat. The strangers carry a message from God: Sarah, old and childless, will have a son. Christians have read this visit in more than one way. Some see God with two angels. Preachers East and West, and later icon painters, came to see in the three a glimpse of the Trinity: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Other pictures of this story show the whole meal, with Abraham and Sarah serving. Rublev leaves them out. He paints only the three, at rest, turned toward one another: no old man with a beard for the Father, but three of the same, sharing one cup. In Orthodox prayer an icon isn't decoration. People pray before it, and some call it a window. Some viewers say the open place is for whoever stands looking. The circle isn't closed. Hebrews puts the old story to work: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Abraham opened his tent. The icon, some say, opens the table.

If you can, pull up a picture of Rublev's Trinity; if not, use the one from the hook, three at a table, one cup, a gap at the front. Let your eyes move slowly around the circle, face to face, then rest on the open side nearest you. If you pray, pray there, at the edge of the table; if not, notice what it's like to be left room.
Rublev's Trinity. An icon of Abraham's three visitors, at rest around one cup, which Christians, especially in the East, read as a picture of the Trinity, with a place at the table left open.
Your line: the open place. Room for one more. See you at the table tomorrow.

829.title: The Black Death
829.hook: plague sweeps Europe; some priests flee, others stay to bury and bless
829.howItsDone: Christians remember the plague years when they pray for the sick and for those who care for them, and Catholic Christians still teach visiting the sick and burying the dead among the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rublev's three visitors with a gap at the front of the table, and your line was the open place.

"Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness." That's from Psalm ninety-one in the King James Bible, a psalm about trusting God when danger is everywhere. In the Middle Ages, a pestilence walked through the towns of Europe in broad daylight. A sickness that came fast, with fever and swellings. Whole households emptied. Markets closed. Graveyards filled, and then there wasn't room. People ran from the cities if they could. And in town after town the same question arrived at the church door: who will come to the sick? Who will hear their last words, and bury them?

People wrote it down while it was happening, and the writers of the time describe priests, doctors and neighbors facing a choice. Some fled. It's hard to blame them; the sickness spread from person to person, and staying could mean dying. But some stayed. Priests went into houses where the sick lay, to hear confession, to anoint, to give the last communion. Monks and nuns nursed people they didn't know. Townspeople carried the dead to be buried when no family was left. Some who stayed caught the sickness and died themselves. Why stay? The answer goes back to the scene we met with Elizabeth of Hungary, the sheep and the goats in Matthew, where the king also says to the righteous, in the King James Bible: "I was sick, and ye visited me". Whatever they did for the least of these, they did for him. Catholic tradition gathered acts like these into a list called the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, and also burying the dead, which comes from the book of Tobit. Protestant churches place Tobit outside their canon, but kept the same command to visit the sick from Matthew. So the plague years hold two stories side by side. One is terror, and flight, and blame, and real cruelty toward people treated as outsiders. The other is quieter, and shorter to tell. Some stayed.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Let the people who stay with the sick come to mind one by one: a nurse finishing a night shift, a doctor making one more call, someone cleaning a hospital room, a chaplain at a bedside, a family member who has given up sleep. If you know one of them by name, let that face come. If you pray, pray for their strength and rest; if not, hold them in your thoughts, and let gratitude sit with them.
Black Death. The plague that swept through Europe in the Middle Ages, when some fled the sick, and some stayed to nurse, bless and bury them.
Your line: some stayed. Priests, monks, nuns, neighbors at the door. Gently, day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: The anchoress's window
830.hook: Julian lived through plague and revolt, and gave counsel through a window to passers-by
830.howItsDone: Christians in several traditions seek out spiritual direction, a regular conversation with an experienced listener about prayer and life, and Julian is sometimes remembered as an early example of that kind of counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Death, when some fled and some stayed with the sick, and your line was some stayed.

A woman from the town of Lynn has come to stand outside a church in Norwich. She is restless, loud in her weeping, and not everyone trusts her. She has visions, she says, and she wants to know whether they come from God or from somewhere else. She doesn't knock on a door. She goes to a window in the wall of a small cell built onto the church, and speaks to the woman inside, who will never come out. The visitor is Margery Kempe. The woman behind the window is the one we call Julian.

On day two hundred seventy-one we met Julian in her cell, and the visions she wrote down. Today, look the other way, out through the window toward the street. Julian's world wasn't quiet. She lived, tradition says, through years of plague and uprising, when angry crowds marched and the powerful struck back. All of that went on outside her wall, and people came to her window carrying it. We know of one visit because Margery Kempe told it in her own book. Margery describes talking with Julian over several days, pouring out her visions, her tears, the things God seemed to be asking of her. Julian's answer, as Margery remembers it, is careful and kind. Paraphrased: test these stirrings by whether they lead you toward the love of God and of your neighbor. The Holy Spirit never moves anyone against charity. Be patient, and don't be shaken by what people say about you. That echoes the First Letter of John, in the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God". Julian didn't tell Margery she was a saint, or a fraud. She gave her a way to tell for herself. And notice what the window asked of Julian. She couldn't go out and fix anyone's life; she could only listen, and answer. Proverbs puts the other side plainly: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." At the window, hearing came first.

Choose one person who might need to talk, a friend going through something, a relative whose calls you let ring, and imagine listening the way Julian did: not fixing, not jumping in, hearing the whole thing. Notice where you'd usually interrupt, and let that urge pass. If you pray, hold them in prayer; if not, hold their voice in mind.
Julian. The anchoress of Norwich who listened and gave counsel through the window of her cell to visitors like Margery Kempe.
Your line: counsel at the window. Not fixing, just hearing the whole matter. That's eight hundred thirty days.

831.title: Catherine and the pope
831.hook: a young laywoman writes to the pope in Avignon and urges him back to Rome
831.carry: if you are what you should be
831.howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read; some Christians who speak up to leaders in church and state look to her example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian at her window, with Margery outside, and your line was counsel at the window.

The pope doesn't live in Rome. For a long stretch of years, the popes have lived in Avignon, in the south of France, in a great palace far from the city of Peter and Paul. In Italy, a young woman from Siena, a wool dyer's daughter, has decided this is wrong. She holds no office and has no title. She isn't a nun in a convent; she lives a life of prayer and service as a laywoman, one of Dominic's lay sisters, in her family's house. And she starts writing letters: to princes, to cardinals, and to the pope himself, telling him, warmly and without flinching, to come home.

Catherine of Siena couldn't easily write, the old accounts say, so she dictated. Her letters went out in Italian, the language she spoke, and they're still read today. They're bold. She calls the pope by a tender family word, something like dear father, and in the same letter tells him plainly to be brave, stop hesitating, and return to Rome. She doesn't flatter him or insult him. She speaks as one Christian to another who happens to hold enormous power, and reminds him what that power is for. She went further than letters: she traveled to Avignon and spoke with him there. And the pope did return to Rome. How much of that was Catherine's doing, historians weigh differently, and the return didn't end the church's troubles; a painful split came soon after. Today the Catholic Church honors her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. A saying handed down under her name is usually given in English like this: if you are what you should be, you will set the whole world on fire. It isn't about being impressive. It's about being true to what you were made for. Jesus says something with the same heat in Luke, in the King James Bible: "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?" In these letters, Catherine's fire was ink, and honesty, and love that wouldn't stay quiet in front of power.

Think of someone who holds power over something you care about, a local official, a manager, a landlord. In your head, find the first honest sentence you'd write them, the way Catherine might: warm, respectful, clear about what needs to change, with no insults and no flattery. If you pray, ask for courage and the right words; if not, let the sentence settle until it sounds like you.
Catherine. A laywoman from Siena who wrote and spoke to the pope in Avignon, warmly and without fear, urging him to return to Rome.
Your line: if you are what you should be. Warm, honest, and unafraid of power. Catch you tomorrow.

832.title: Bridget of Sweden
832.hook: a widow, mother of a large family, founder, and visionary of the passion
832.howItsDone: Catholics honor Bridget of Sweden as a saint and one of the patron saints of Europe, and Bridgettine sisters still live and pray in houses that trace back to her order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena wrote to the pope in Avignon, and your line was if you are what you should be.
screen: `IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.`

segments.voice: What does a woman do when the life she built is suddenly over? In Sweden, a noblewoman has spent her married years running a household, raising a large family, serving at the royal court. Tradition says she and her husband went on pilgrimage together, and not long after, he died. She is a widow now, her children growing up. She could step back into a quiet widowhood. Instead, her work is about to begin. She will found a religious order, travel to Rome and never really come home, and write down visions that people still read.

Bridget, or Birgitta in Swedish, didn't become a nun and disappear. She became something harder to describe. After her husband's death she gave herself to prayer, and visions came again and again. Her early biographers say she had one even as a child; now they filled her life. They kept returning to the passion of Christ: his suffering on the cross, and his mother Mary standing near it. They were gathered into books called her Revelations, full of the cross seen up close, painful and tender. She founded a religious order, often called the Bridgettines, with a great house at Vadstena in Sweden. Like Catherine, she wrote to the popes in Avignon and urged them back to Rome. She went to Rome herself, lived there for years, and died there. One of her daughters, Catherine of Sweden, stayed with her and is honored as a saint too. The Bible pays particular attention to widows. In Luke, when the infant Jesus is brought to the temple, an old widow named Anna is there, who, the King James Bible says, "departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Widowhood, in that picture, isn't only loss; it can be a new kind of service. James is just as blunt about everyone else's part: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction". Catholics honor Bridget as a saint and a patron of Europe. Her life holds both a widow's grief and a widow's strength.
screen: `AN ORDER, AND A HOUSE AT VADSTENA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has lost a husband or a wife, a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend's mother, recently or long ago, and think about their days now: the meals, the empty side of the bed, the quiet evenings. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in your thoughts, with care.

833.howItsDone: Christians today read the Bible in their own languages, at home and aloud in worship, and Wycliffe's translation is remembered as part of the long story of putting scripture into ordinary speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bridget of Sweden, whose real work began when she was widowed, and your line was a widow's strength.

Set the scene this way. A man stands at the edge of a field in England, leaning on his plough, while someone reads to him from a small handwritten book. The words are the Gospels, and this time he understands them, because they're in English. In his parish church the readings come in Latin, the language of scholars and priests. He has heard about the Bible all his life. Now he's hearing it. Behind that little book stands an Oxford scholar named John Wycliffe, and the followers who carried his work on.

John Wycliffe taught at Oxford, and grew convinced of something that sounds simple and was explosive: ordinary Christians should be able to read the scriptures for themselves, in their own language. He criticized the church's wealth and argued that scripture should judge the church, not the other way around. His followers, sometimes called Lollards, set out to put the whole Bible into English. They worked from the church's Latin Bible, and every copy was written by hand, because printing hadn't come to England yet. Copies spread among townspeople and country folk. Church authorities in England saw danger in it: errors, divisions, unrest. Before long, making or owning a new English translation without a bishop's approval was forbidden, and some caught with these books were punished. Christians still weigh that history differently. Some see the church protecting people from mistakes; others see it keeping the word from them. But the hope behind the work is very old. At Pentecost, in Acts, a crowd from many nations hears the apostles, and the King James Bible gives their astonished question: "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" That's this week's thread too: Sergius sharing bread at the forest's edge, Rublev leaving a place open, priests who stayed with the sick, Julian at her window, Catherine writing to the pope, Bridget beginning again as a widow. Faith brought out onto ordinary ground. Wycliffe's followers brought the book itself.

Pick one short passage, the opening of John's Gospel or a psalm if you don't know where to start, and read it once quietly. Then read it again, aloud if you can, letting each word land as if you'd never heard it in your own language before, the way that ploughman did. If you pray, let the words become your prayer; if not, stay with whichever word stops you.
Wycliffe's Bible. The handwritten English Bible made by John Wycliffe's followers from the Latin, so ordinary people could hear scripture in their own tongue.
Your line: the ploughman's bible. Every man in his own tongue. A week's end, day eight hundred thirty-three.

fork.setup: you're a scholar who believes ordinary people should read the Bible in their own language, but the church reads it in Latin. what do you do?
options: keep it in Latin and explain it in sermons.
put it into English, and let copies spread.

chat.says: Why was it such a big deal to have the Bible in English back then?
options: Church readings were in Latin; Wycliffe's followers copied it by hand so ordinary people could hear it.
English Bibles were already everywhere; Wycliffe just made a cheaper printed edition.
The church had no Bible in any language, so Wycliffe wrote the very first one himself.
chat.meaning: Wycliffe held that ordinary Christians should read scripture in their own language; his followers copied it into English by hand, from the Latin.
